doc.title: Nick Brignola interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 28, 1997

title: Competition for work and respect among musicians
summary: He tells students at clinics they will compete with veterans for gigs, balanced by respect among peers.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, why not? We’ll start it up anew. Was there competition, and is there still a lot of competition to get what work is out there?

Oh yeah, sure. I mean there’s only so much out there and now you’ve got all these music schools releasing these kids that are great musicians you know, in many respects more well prepared for certain gigs then I’ll ever be prepared for. But when I used to go do clinics I used to make mention of the fact, I’d say, “Listen, after you leave school here and you’re all prepared and you’re ready to go do your thing, just remember that guys like me, and there’s a whole mess of us out there waiting for you guys. And just remember, we’re all after the same gig. So you’d better be ready.” And when I first started to say that I was trying to tell them that it’s not going to be easy, that once you get out there you’re competing with everybody and anything. In school now you’re only competing with little Johnny or little Ethel on the alto for the first chair in the band and all that, that’s a simple situation. When you get out in the world, now it’s like everything’s up for grabs, and are you ready for that. That was my message. But then it got to the point where it was like I got thinking, I said wait a minute there are so many gigs, I’m going to kill this kid when he comes out. You know, I’m not going to let him get that job, you know. And then I would tell them that. I’d say, “When you come out, it’s like a boxing match. I’m going to knock your brains out so you’d better be ready to beat me up, you know, because I’m going to take your job.” And they would sit there and shake and the music teacher would come up to me later and say, “Hey, what’d you tell them that for?” And then some of them would say, “Boy I’m glad you told them that.” Because really that’s what it’s about.
Sure and they’ve been doing that for years, I mean the Kansas City tenor battles and all of that.

That’s the way the music was brought up. There is a competition, yeah. But it’s also a respect too. There’s a competition but when you know you’re in the room with the same kind of maybe not the exact — how can you equate talent — but I mean when you’re among company that you know at least as your equal or maybe better than you or a little bit less than you, there’s a respect there that, I mean that’s the way I feel, I don’t know how other people feel. But I always have that respect for people. And yeah, I’m going to knock your brains out, but when the game’s over, we’re going to sit around and hang and tell stories and have a good time. Sometimes it’s not like that. It’s a very vicious, personal thing, and I think that’s when it gets lost somewhere.
